Course 05

Communication and relationships

Listening, requests, agreements and boundaries.

Lesson 4. Setting boundaries

1 · Lesson

A boundary is a way of saying what we are and are not willing to do. Social skills psychology distinguishes three styles: passive (keeping quiet about what I need to avoid conflict), aggressive (imposing what I need without regard for the other) and assertive (expressing what I need while respecting the other).

Assertiveness can be learned. Some useful techniques: the broken record (calmly repeating the same idea without getting drawn into side arguments), fogging (acknowledging the other's partial point without giving way on the essentials) and saying "no" without endless explanations.

Setting boundaries can cause guilt at first, especially if we are used to pleasing others. But relationships in which things can be said tend to be more stable than those in which resentment builds up.

2 · Example

A colleague asks you, for the third time this week, to stay late and cover for him. Passive: "OK…" (and you seethe inside). Aggressive: "Always the same, you take advantage!" Assertive: "I can't this week. If you need me to cover another day, let me know in advance and we'll see."

3 · Activity

Think of a situation in which you find it hard to say no. Write a short assertive sentence for next time. Rehearse it aloud a couple of times: saying it aloud makes it easier when the moment comes.
